I think this is just barely a Not Recommended, in a vacuum I could easily recommend it, but since the first game exists, I feel this just takes too many steps backwards. While I do like a lot of what this game did, most positive reviews have already mentioned what I like, so I'm instead going to list gripes, because this is far from a perfect game. Most of my gripes are either similar to the first game or the same but maybe worse. So here goes:

-General game balance feels worse. Movement speed is still busted. I am glad they removed double dashing, it was too much in the first game. I am glad they made Athena's boons much rarer, deflect is too OP. That said, this game goes utterly crazy with dodge chance and sprint speed. You can beat any of the boss fights so easily by just getting a blue or rarer sprint increase boon, and literally just run past their attacks. The squirrel pet that gives you dodge chance, movespeed and free blocks every encounter is just absurdly broken. You can also just pick up a mercury common boon that massively slow down enemy projectiles.. the % decrease is also absurd and not balanced at all. I don't understand these design choices, it makes the game way too easy, it negates way too much of the mechanics you're supposed to be playing around. Also almost forgot to mention, why does freeze exist? I see you can't fully freeze bosses but it also just makes the hallways so ridiculously easy and still slows the bosses, picking up any other boon for your cast feels like a waste.

-Pacing is awkward at many parts of the game. The rate at which you unlock things seems too arbitrary and not intentional enough. The game seems to try and intentionally slow you down at points, kind of lazy.

-Visual design is still overly busy at many times. It is not always clear what is part of the environment, which sprites are enemies, which are random vfx, which are enemies projectiles, which are your own resources or positive effects, etc. Ironically I think they made the traps in Tartarus too visible compared to first game, while everything else in the environment is just often too vibrant and in-your-face. I think they did a better job on enemy visual design, to distinguish enemies and their attack patterns. But environments and vfx, they've overdone it in many spots.

-Way too many resource systems. I understand, roguelike, yadda yadda but this game is addicted to them and it all contributes to inability to balance. I think the arcana cards were my favorite, but most of the other stuff, a LOT of it could and should be cut.

-The writing team has once again chosen quantity over quality. No, writers at Supergiant, I am not impressed that you recorded 600 different 3-paragraph voicelines for 2000 different possible interactions of inconsequential things happening.. please stop this, it was also one of my main gripes with the first game.

-A lot of the story is contrived, and especially the ending is incredibly stupid. I will avoid direct spoilers I suppose but I will just say, Hecate may be the only sensible character in this whole story. The main antagonist is a colossal idiot and the protagonist turns into an even bigger idiot.

EDIT: FEW MORE THINGS:
- For a game I put 45 hours into, I got a like a small handful of chuckles at some of the humor. Most of it was not funny, overly millennial coded, like a lot of it is getting close to Borderlands 3 levels.
- Darren Korb is VERY hit or miss here. Like the main menu theme and stuff from the trailers is great.. then you get in game and some of the tracks are just jarring or straight up annoying, don't understand it.

I really love this game. The combat retains the feel of the original but adds a twist with new mechanics. Visually, it is stunning, and there are plenty of special interactions and events to discover between NPCs. The music is so beautiful that I’ve been playing it on repeat on Spotify.

Hades II is one of those games that makes me deeply suspicious of the concept of a “sequel.” Usually, when a game is as beloved as Hades, following it up presents a simple problem: how on earth do you improve upon something that already feels damn near perfected? Supergiant Games apparently responded by shrugging, putting a witch in the Underworld, giving her an unreasonable quantity of magical weapons, and deciding that Greek mythology did not contain enough family drama already, and needed a father of all monsters to turn Mount Olympus into a HIKING trail lmao.

After everything I’ve experienced in Hades II, I can confidently say that this is not merely a sequel attempting to recreate the magic of its predecessor. It is a remarkably ambitious expansion of the entire formula, introducing new characters, environments, combat systems, routes, mechanics, and enough mythology to make keeping track of who is related to whom feel like a second gameplay mechanic. XD Hades II follows Melinoë, the younger sister of Zagreus, as she attempts to overthrow Chronos, the Titan of Time who has seized control of the Underworld. Rather than retracing Zagreus’ escape attempt, Melinoë repeatedly breaks into the Underworld, fighting toward Chronos. And somehow, Supergiant has made that premise feel natural. Well, mostly natural. This is still Hades II, after all, so naturally there is also a King Vermin named Uh-Oh who is apparently hellbent on exacting revenge for whatever Zagreus did to his ancestors in the first game. Because apparently even the rats have generational grudges now lol!

The basic structure remains recognisably Hades: enter a run, fight through procedurally arranged encounters, collect Boons and resources, assemble increasingly ridiculous combinations of abilities, get obliterated by something you were certain you had under control, return home, talk to everyone, upgrade yourself, and convince yourself that the next attempt will definitely be different. I've learnt it the hard way lol, it will not be different. You will die again. But you will have three new conversations waiting for you, so technically you won. ;) That is the brilliance of Hades II. Failure is never simply failure. Every run feeds into progression through resources, Arcana, weapons, incantations, relationships, prophecies, familiars, or simply discovering another piece of dialogue.

And then there is Melinoë herself. Where Zagreus felt like a fast, aggressive warrior constantly improvising through danger, Melinoë feels much more deliberate. Her combat revolves around positioning, magical control and Magick, with her Cast creating a binding area that can hold enemies in place. Suddenly, you aren't merely asking, “What can I hit?” You are asking, “Where do I want everything to be when I hit it?” Which is a surprisingly sophisticated question for someone who is about to turn a room full of monsters into artistic paste. XD Her Omega attacks push this further. Holding an attack or ability allows Melinoë to channel a more powerful version, consuming Magick for enhanced effects. Of course, accidentally holding the wrong button and spending all your Magick on one humble enemy means experiencing the ancient Greek tragedy known as “skill issue.” Very prominent in Homer's books I can concur lol.

The weapons give Melinoë distinct playstyles, while their alternate aspects ensure they are not simply interchangeable stat sticks. Some encourage close-range aggression, others reward distance and positioning, while others turn the battlefield into a particularly violent mathematics equation. And then Boons enter the equation. Hades II remains magnificent at allowing individual mechanics to collide into increasingly absurd combinations. Sometimes they give you exactly what you need. Sometimes they give you three abilities that have absolutely no business being in the same build. And sometimes the game looks directly into your soul and decides that this run will be about fishing and fishing only, and you better enjoy it lmao!

The greatest expansion, however, comes from the world itself. Hades II gives Melinoë multiple destinations, including the Surface, creating a much broader structure for each run. Instead of a single linear descent, your journey can branch into radically different environments, enemies and challenges. The Underworld still possesses that familiar Hades identity, but the Surface introduces an entirely different atmosphere. Ephyra feels alive in contrast with the Underworld's enclosed environments, while later regions escalate the visual and mechanical spectacle further. The Surface especially feels like Supergiant asking, “What if we took everything you learned underground and then made you do it somewhere much less comfortable?” Apparently the answer is fire. Lots of fire. And enemies who would very much like you to experience all of it personally and generously enough, free of charge! XD

The bosses are another highlight. Hades has always understood that a good roguelike boss needs to test something specific about how you have been playing, rather than simply possessing a large health bar. Hades II expands upon this with encounters that test positioning, timing, crowd control and resource management. I mean, Supergiant turned a malevolent set of Sirens from Homer's Odyssey into a new up and coming rock band that prefer introducing you to their music physically! XD Some fights become chaotic spectacles, while others force you to learn patterns and resist the instinct to throw every ability you have at the nearest moving object, which happens quite occasionally lol.

One of the game's greatest strengths remains its writing. Supergiant manages to turn a cast of mythological figures into characters who feel remarkably human without stripping away their mythological identities. Characters remember what you have done, comment on your progress, react to things you wouldn't expect them to notice, and go accompany you while you down the liquor stock of Mount Olympus! XD Because death is so deeply integrated into the structure of the game, returning home after a failed run doesn't feel like hitting a narrative reset button. It feels like coming back to a household that has continued existing while you were away. Melinoë's relationships with Hecate, her family and Chronos give the sequel its own emotional identity, with a stronger emphasis on inherited responsibility, family history and the consequences of what came before her. Which is impressive considering how many characters in this family tree have unresolved issues that probably require several centuries of therapy, and we're the unlucky therapist who gets to deal with their problems by spurning one of them, receiving the blessing of another, and going through purgatory until the one you scorned realises you're not that bad after all lol.

Then finally there is Darren Korb's soundtrack, that of which will result in you unwillingly yelling out Scylla and the Sirens as they perform their new single like a deranged choirboy lol. Some encounters are accompanied by music so energetic that you begin fighting enemies with approximately 400% more confidence than your actual abilities justify. This turns out not to be the safest situation lol. The music says: “You are an immortal witch blessed by the gods.” The boss says: “You have 11 health and are running towards me at mach 10.” XD

Overall, Hades II is an extraordinary sequel, an exceptional roguelike, and another absurdly polished demonstration of why Supergiant Games can take a genre built around repetition and make it feel like an endless process of discovery. I highly recommend Hades II, and it has earned its place among the games I will happily return to long after I have finished pretending that my next run will be the one where everything goes according to plan. It inevitably won't. But hey, at least the gods will have something to laugh about lol! ;)

TL;DR

One of the best rogue-likes and sequels out there. I played the hell out of the incredible first game and somehow this one perfects the base formula even more while adding on multiple new and refreshing systems. I did not play it in early access so I can't speak to those experiences. I purchased it with a small sale but believe it is well worth the price with tons of replayability. If you played the first game and enjoyed it, PLEASE play this one. You won't be disappointed. 

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hades 2 had been in early access for a quite a while and I was not keeping up with its updates or release window. When the 2026 Summer Sale came around and I spotted it on discount, I felt it was about time to pick it up. There are a lot of games in early access nowadays, with most turning out to be labors of love after finally releasing the 1.0 update. For this game, I decided to wait until that time, not because I heard bad things (because there were none that I could find), but mainly because I wanted to experience the game in its final form without any comparisons. I can confidently say that I am glad I did because the game did not disappoint, and even exceeded my expectations. 

A lot of the core systems return from the past games such as different weapons, keepsakes, heat difficulty (now re-named to fear), etc. I was curious and worried to see where the story was going to go since the first game's epilogue concluded well in my opinion and some sequels can feel more like cash grabs. This luckily is not one of those sequels. The story feels at the center of this game, and I liked that. Just like the first game, there’s multiple side stories and quests with returning and new characters alike, which was awesome to see. I obviously missed the House of Hades and its different rooms and features, but the Crossroads did a great job at mimicking those similar feelings of the past game (I still miss the head chef tho, but the broker returning made up for it).

I think my first wow moment of this game was when I returned to the crossroads to begin a run and was introduced to the arcana cards system. Similar in a way to the Mirror of the Night from the first game, but with its own unique twist of building your own deck of cards. It was even cooler to see more and more of the cards unlocked over time, wondering how you can meet requirements to activate your most valuable cards and some bonus ones. 

My second wow moment of this game came directly after my introduction to arcana cards when I saw there were two paths I could choose at the start of a run: one for the underworld and one for the surface? I expected the surface to be more for things related to story beats, similar to the first game after meeting Persephone. I wanted to do everything I could to unlock this as soon as possible as my mind raced with what could be up there, and when I made it, I was not disappointed. The surface was a whole new area with different enemies, bosses, and friendly NPC’s to interact with similar to Eurydice, Achilles, etc. from the first game. The underworld had these NPC’s too, but the surface even had a different final boss with unique mechanics. Wow, just wow. My driving force for most of the game's story was seeing if characters from the first game would return after defeating Chronos and Typhon (you will have to beat the game to find that out). 

The more I progressed through the story and tried out new weapons and keepsakes, I kept thinking things like, “Where is this one god? They were really cool and I wish they would come back”, “that frog is so cute! It would be cool if you could have it as a pet”, “why would I ever use this keepsake, weapon, or arcana card? They dont seem very good.” It started to freak me out at one point because every time I had one of these thoughts, they were quickly put to rest. I was so excited to see some of my personal favorite returning gods like Artemis, Athena, and Dionysus but this time with their own unique twists. New gods like Hephaestus, Hera, and Selene also became my new favorites. The same can also be said for friendly NPC’s like Narcissus, Arachne, Circe, etc. Every character felt somehow familiar but also refreshing.

I felt a similar sense of joy when pets or Animal Familiars were introduced and I could finally have Frinos the Frog as my loyal companion. Finding out you could upgrade your pets AND customize them was just the cherry on top. Even the planting and harvesting of resources was a welcome addition, too. Finally, the introduction of chaos trials answered my question of some keepsakes and arcana cards' usefulness. Using certain combinations like the White Antler keepsake with the Aspect of Artemis, or Aspect of Circe with arcana cards like The Furies and The Unseen made me realise that any build is viable. Not only this, but it made me remember why I loved the first game so much. 

One of my favorite questlines was bringing peace to the soul of Odysseus, mainly because I had just recently seen The Odyssey movie in theatres and felt like a kid at Disney each time I saw these characters from the famous story appear in the game. It brought me back to reading Percy Jackson too when I saw a villain like Chronos appear. When the main story concluded, I decided to work towards the epilogue and remaining achievements, which I am glad I did. It uncovered other questlines I would have never known existed otherwise and tied up loose ends nicely just like the first game. These ancient Greek tales of the gods exemplified in this game sparked my curiosity to the point of purchasing books in real life to learn more about how they came to be and their underlying messages or lessons. When a game influences me in real life ways, that's when I know it is special. 

Supergiant Games, you truly outdid yourself with this sequel and series. The amount of effort and passion is truly noticeable in every aspect of the game: the art style, voice acting, music, combat, weapons, dialogue, etc. Perhaps the biggest thing that stuck out to me was I don't think I ever noticed a single line of repeated dialogue from any character in my playthrough. I am confident there are repeated lines and maybe I was not paying close enough attention, but the time it must have taken to write and record so many lines is extremely commendable. I am sure I missed some important things like story beats or the ranking system near the end of the game, and honestly? I might still keep the game downloaded to play now and then when I’m bored as the gameplay loop is just that enjoyable. If you have played the first and are questioning playing the second game, don't wait any longer. You will have to experience this greatness yourself.

As a game, Hades 2 is a massive improvement over its predecessor: it has better pacing and progression, better and more numerous weapons and powerups, better resource management, better difficulty balance, a greater general variety and even multiple routes to complete. Not a single aspect of the whole game made me miss the previous installment gameplay-wise, it's just so much better and enjoyable to play, and that is saying a lot since the first Hades was already a great game.

Unfortunately, the same cannot be said regarding the narrative and the characters' writing. The premises are very interesting and compelling and the story unfolds smoothly right up to the ending, then it all falls apart in a rather anti-climatic way. The conclusion feels way too simplistic and convenient considering what's at stake, and a lot of the sub plots get a resolution that feels either inconsequential or disappointing. I have kept playing after the main ending in order to complete the optional challenges, and even after meeting [spoiler]the Fates[/spoiler] and seeing the "true" ending I was let down.

Artistically the game is still impeccable, I love most of the Gods' redesigned portraits as well as the newly introduced characters' ones, graphics are polished and vibrant, music is top notch as always... Only the story feels lacking. That, and some characters are just plain dull and they have really poor interactions with the player. Yeah, talking about you, Nemesis.

Luckily the game is still so fun and addictive to play that it will make you forget about these shortcomings, so if you enjoyed the original Hades and/or like roguelikes in general it's still a must play.

My second favourite game of 2025!

There are reasons as to why it's not number one, though. The major one being the writing; While good throughout large parts of the game - the banter between characters, narrator, and Melinoë is especially excellent - the conclusion to the story is lackluster, I felt like both Mel and the player are stripped of agency during the most important parts (and I'm not only talking about the main ending, but the epilogue as well - that was some real [b] BS[/b], at least for me).

I know starting off with the worst aspect of a game, that took over my life for a whole month last year, looks quite weird, but the resolution of the story really soured my experience - which as I said was fantastic! (for the most part)

Other sides of the game, beginning with gameplay! It, is, great. The dash took a couple hours to grow accustomed to, but in the end, I enjoyed my time with Hades II much more than with the first one; Even though, I already was fond of that one.

The music and the graphics, as expected, are outstanding. Nothing more to add here.

I didn't find the resource gathering bad. It was fine, done in such a way that didn't hinder my playthrough. Although if someone was to be way faster than me, I could see them finding this system very annoying.

In conclusion, this game is great and worth playing. The art, the music, majority of the writing, the gameplay are all exceptional. However the game's writing does feel like it was constrained by the name itself 'Hades'; It is limited by Greek mythology. While the first game's story felt natural and self-contained, Hades II's narrative feels forced at time and like it's trying too hard to be larger than first Hades.

After I 100%ed Hades a few years ago, I left a review for the game describing it as a masterpiece. In that same review, which happens to be my most popular review to date, I made a few requests and a small wishlist for Hades II, which at the time wasn't even announced. I asked for more gods, more game modes, more storylines, and pretty much more of everything we had seen in Hades. To nobody's surprise, Supergiant delivered. Hades II is basically everything we absolutely adored about Hades, but bigger and better in most cases. Even though I undoubtedly consider both games to be masterpieces and easily two of my favorite games of all time, I have to say that there are very few things, two to be precise, which Hades II does worse than its predecessor. More specifically, the main story, which admittedly wasn't as captivating as the original, and the boons you get offered by the gods. I will stay away from the main story to avoid spoilers, but I will discuss my opinion on the boons in the game. In Hades, every boon you found or got offered was pretty consistent mythologically speaking. For example, Artemis, the goddess of the hunt, her boons would focus on critical chance. Makes sense, right? She hunts from the shadows, sneak attack, critical multiplier, makes sense. Aphrodite, the goddess of love, her boons would focus on applying the status effect 'weak' and the damage you do to enemies who are close to you. Again, makes perfect sense, when someone is in love with you, they lay down their arms and armor, leaving them exposed and weak, metaphorically speaking, of course. Such consistencies also made creating a build much easier, as you always knew which god to go for depending on what you needed. In Hades II, however, the boons you get offered by the gods are very inconsistent. For example, Hephaestus, the god of smithing, is somehow able to offer you a boon which raises your max HP based on how much magicka you currently have. Or Hestia, the goddess of the fireplace, is somehow able to offer you a boon which raises your dodge chance. Or Ares, the god of war, being by far the weakest god in the game, as most of his boons focus on picking up blood off the ground which slightly raises your movement and attack speed. I personally feel like they had some very fun ideas for some boons, but didn't have a god in the game who would be able to represent them, therefore they just slapped them onto the god that would make the most sence, which in some cases ended up making no sence regardless. In no way does this make Hades II worse, absolutely not. It's just something I noticed while playing. Either way, after fully 100%ing both games, and having an immense amount of fun, I can confidently say that they are special, and every action / roguelike fan should experience them.

An astounding sequel to the already incredible predecessor, Hades. Coming from someone who's soaked 100+ hours into this game along with obtained every trophy, it was a beautifully challenging and heartfelt game that blended combat and dialogue just as well as the first game if not better, and raised the stakes tremendously while keeping the theme genuine and relatable, that being the complexities of family.

To start, I'd like to talk about the revitalized weapon and strengthening portion. Each weapon in your arsenal is gradually unlocked and work to aid varying playstyles akin to Hades I, however, with new weapons and aspects (which are essentially sub-categories of the main weapons), you are able to explore even greater combination alongside boons. Speaking of which, boons were GREATLY improved in Hades II, as no specific god feels either too powerful or powerless and the chance for legendary or duo boons (synergized boons between gods), have been increased to make you feel disgustingly undefeatable. Though the bosses have been empowered just as much.

Which brings me to my next point, the difficulty. Some find it too ruthless while others consider it enjoyable.  Where you stand is perfectly acceptable, however Hades II handles the progression of enemies and bosses as effectively as the first game. With unique enemy designs and nigh unforgettable bosses, with each loss, a piece of them is stuck with you to learn, and through time and effort, a method to the madness can be seen. Furthermore, if you're crazy enough to pursue Vows, (game changes to increase difficulty), the learning curve is just as satisfying, the Vow of Rivals especially, all working together to make the replayability skyrocket.

And finally, the most intricate portion arguably, are the story-line, characters, and how they interact with one another and the world. In spite of their mythical status, the gods and cursed beings you'll meet as you End Time will each have their own unique personalities, and when I say this, I don't mean silly gimmicks, but rather genuine, compound people that have their own lives, and through the hundreds of dialogue recorded, you are able to see into their lives, their fears, their general perspectives that feel almost realistic to their context. And finally, through that dialogue and story-lines show the difficult relationships they have with each other, and the companions which hold dear to the protagonist and highlights the quote, "Home is not where you live, But who cares when you're gone."

Ultimately, Hades II is an incredible sequel that defies not only expectation but the fates themselves as the multifaceted aspects combine to provide a game worthy of praise, and show the potential that lies in all of us to fight for who we love, and the fact that wounds are not to be look upon in abjection, but rather as a lesson to be told to others as it gently heals.

P.S. I left ALOT out of this review, but if I tried to explain further, I'd be writing this review for a lot longer than I need to

This game is a lot richer than its predecessor and has many more fun mechanics and items to play around with. I also appreciate that there are two different paths, as it breaks the monotony and can be refreshing. The same goes for the open-field area in the underground.

However, the top side is unfortunately very bad, in my opinion, for multiple reasons. Specifically, the Mount and Summit. The first two regions are great, especially the first one. Once you start the mountain climb, though, it falls apart. Yes, the difficulty is ridiculously dialed up, but that is not my main issue.

My main issue is the boss and level design.

Since it is essentially two regions in one, it becomes very monotonous, and that is made considerably worse by the fact that almost every encounter has the same enemies and takes place in the same kind of boxed-in room. It is tight and creates an absolute mess of visual clutter and enemy numbers without giving you much freedom of movement, which seriously hampers any kind of strategy beyond spraying and praying for the most part.

The bosses are also very lame.

Prometheus will literally stop the fight to play a memory game with you, which is both concentration and immersion-breaking, while also being far too punishing if you miss one, or god forbid, multiple sequences. It can burn through a bunch of your revives. That sequence should automatically end if you trigger a Death Defiance.

The Summit throws multiple hard-hitting bosses at you without giving you any real chance to recuperate or heal before going into the final boss. And that final boss is atrocious.

The fight itself is long and boring. It is essentially a damage sponge where you find yourself running up, throwing a cast and getting a few hits in, then running around, and repeating that ad infinitum. It is so lame that after beating him the first few times, I was reluctant and dreading having to redo that fight. It is simply not fun.

There is challenging difficulty, and then there is cheap difficulty. In a lot of cases, the Summit falls into the latter. That is especially disappointing because the vast majority of the rest of the game is fantastic.

There is so much I want to love about this sequel, but that Mount + Summit section really puts a sour taste in my mouth.

Unrelated side note: I kind of wish all the small talk you have with the gods and companions would actually result in something definitive. It can be fun from a lore perspective, but at the end of the day, you know nothing will come out of all the talking. It is just talk for the sake of talking.

Probably one of the best Rogue-Likes and definitely a massive landmark in the genre similarly to the original Hades, if you enjoyed the first one this is an improvement in almost every conceivable way. I think perhaps my biggest criticism would be directed at the story and the protagonist, Hades 2 is tonally a much more serious and a higher stakes affair than 1 which isn't inherently bad but it positions Melinoe as a character that has to be a lot more grounded, serious and duty-driven than what we grew used to with Zagreus, that's not to say she is devoid of personality, far from it and she mostly serves as a big foil to most of all the other eccentric personalities in the game which serves her quite well and aids her development and exploration further.

But it's all just not as captivating as the first game, Zagreus' endeavor was fundamentally relatable throughout the entire game with Zagreus himself as a rebellious young adult standing up to his father, eventually leading up to the mending of his family. It was simply more personal and while not relatable in the literal sense of the conflict the overarching intimate familial themes surrounding a lot of the characters and the core conflict of the story felt very real and humanizing. That's not to say the game lacks any of this, it's quite there and very potently at times, its left an impression on me for sure, but as an overall experience to go through as opposed to just its great heights it's not as captivating as I in that regard.

It's worth noting that the game has customizable permanent upgrades through not just the arcana but also weapon upgrades, this goes hand in hand with the Will of the Night (This game's improved version of the Pact of Punishment), while I am a huge fan of this system it's worth pointing out that even if the game pushes many, many incentives for you to keep upping the difficulty as you get stronger, many players may not feel compelled to do so leading to a pretty unengaging experience that may lead some away, as for some people it's not all enticing to willingly opt into these challenges. But again I personally enjoy them and keep doing them for fun. 

I think another thing to keep in mind about Hades 2 and sincerely about Hades as a whole is that it's not really the kind of Rogue-Like centered around big flashy moments and broken runs, you'll never reach heights as such as Isaac where each and every single tear you fire is a nuclear bomb. The game has a much more reserved pool of "Items" (Boons) but where it shines is the agency you get to exercise over the boons you get and what boons you do, broken runs in Hades aren't always these high dopamine flashing color game breaking experiences but more so rewards for clever building. In other words as opposed to Isaac where you make do with what you're given, Hades 2 encourages you to find out what works with what, this is especially apparent with the mechanics behind certain boons and duo boons only being available after certain ones are picked since they rely on a previous one being in your build. There have been many times where I've neglected a boon or even a weapon and playstyle altogether because to me it seemed lame, only to decidedly attempt a run building around these and absolutely crush the game (Aspect of Artemis I owe you an apology). To anyone reading this I'd encourage you not just to make do but to experiment, be creative and try to see all the combinations that may yield something amazing.

The point I'm making is that one of Hades' 2 biggest strength is being a very sandbox-y rogue-like experience where if you're willing, every run can feel like taking another crack at a lab to experiment and do something new, where you get to decide how hard the game is and in turn are rewarded for it, I personally gravitate to more railroaded curated experiences and generally think these are best but Hades 2 is definitely a king of accessibility no doubt.

TL:DR - Probably one of the most brilliantly designed games following the steps of its boundary pushing predecessor, wish I had felt more of a connection with Melinoe like I did with Zagreus but overall still an incredible experience.

Seeing their next game be a sequel to their most recent - and most successful - outing, it seemed like my goats had fallen for the bag.

I was happily proven wrong. Hades 2 is more than worthy as a successor, improving on the original in (almost) every single way. It is the most polished, most refined version of what Supergiant has proven themselves masters of. The broadest cast of well written, well performed, wonderfully drawn characters, who - despite their apparent divinity - are deeply human and relevant in struggle and tone. 

Not only are they written well, they are written broadly, and extensively; as such making the interactions in this game some of the most responsive in any video game ever. One of the greatest strengths of the medium is to have dialogue with the player, to respond when poked, and to poke back. The levels to which this game recognises your choices is frankly absurd, and I can only imagine the spreadsheets and programming needed in order to organise such a thing. Using a specific keepsake, in a specific difficulty level, against a specific boss, having done something specific on the night before - so much of what you do is accounted for, and I was constantly impressed by the lengths this game goes to answer the question “I wonder if they have dialogue for that?” with a resounding “YES!”

The combat is also greatly increased, with more flexibility and buildcrafting than before, offering a wide array of weapons, each with several aspects that really change how you play the game. Such an arsenal, when combined with the Arcana Cards, Animal Familiars, Keepsakes, broad pantheon of deities, each with their own boons, upgrades, and synergies therein - this ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ DWARFS the first game in terms of variety and replayablity, and that’s even before addressing that there are two separate routes. There is a hell of a lot of meat on this bone.

The story is the one fault I would make. It just isn’t as compelling as the original, it has more limbs, but lacks the simplicity and heart of the first, and I found the ending to be pretty disappointing and underwhelming. I understand that you write yourself into a corner when it comes to narrative and roguelikes, but it still fell pretty flat.

Despite it’s overarching narrative shortcomings, Hades 2 more than justifies its existence with its levels of polish, detail, replayability, and charm. The music and characters and art direction is still top of class, unbeatable, and further reinforces Supergiant’s status as legendary.

If what you loved about Hades was its fast combat, simple progression, aggressive playstyle, and constant momentum, Hades II feels like a step backward. The original game was focused. You fought, made meaningful choices, improved your build, and kept moving. Hades II adds more systems, more resources, more interruptions, and more layers between you and the combat.

Mechanics

The combat is slower and more restrictive. Melinoë relies much more on Magick, Casts, charged Omega attacks, and setup, which constantly breaks the flow that made Zagreus so satisfying to play. On top of that, the game piles on currencies, gathering tools, gardening, incantations, familiars, Arcana cards, Hexes, crafting, and temporary systems like Arachne's dress armor. I eventually stopped caring about most of it and started skipping whatever I could just to get back to fighting. The cast and Hex convolute the boon pull and force you to use them not to mention 9/10 I am drawing hex or cast. Everything has a gotcha, if you get some kind of actual buff to attack, it comes with a penalty or a chance roll making most of them feel pointless. 

Story and Progression

Hades made its roguelike structure feel natural because Zagreus repeatedly trying to escape the Underworld made sense within the story. Hades II feels less consistent. Hecate is the clearest example. She is training Melinoë to defeat Chronos, yet after you spend an entire area collecting armor, upgrades, and resources, she fights you as a boss and burns through the exact things you are supposed to preserve for the real threat ahead. The game needs a boss there, but the story does not justify it nearly as well as the first game did.

Design

The artwork is still excellent, but the design direction feels increasingly disconnected from the Greek mythology underneath it. The witchcraft aesthetic is pushed so hard through dresses, familiars, cauldrons, gardening, rituals, spell systems, and occult styling that it starts to become the identity of the game rather than one part of the setting. Chaos is the worst example for me. The original felt ancient, alien, and detached. Now Chaos looks like an eccentric Femboi, trying to be fashion model in a 1940s pantsuit, which strips away much of what made the character feel primordial now he is in the wrong time all together. Hermes has a similar problem with him being Asian out of nowhere, why change the desgin? I do not expect museum accurate depictions, but some of these redesigns feel like the modern aesthetic is taking priority over the mythology itself which was part of the draw, for me.

Overall

Hades II has more content, more mechanics, and more progression systems, but more is not automatically better. Hades was focused. Hades II feels bloated. The combat is slower, the progression is more cluttered, the story is less consistent, and the visual direction feels further removed from the mythological foundation of the first game.

A quite good rogue-like, especially due to it's graphics and a good-feeling battle mechanic. There are a lot of small things, which make this an overall good game, but I want to mark out the following three, which probably weren't mentioned this often:
1. It prevents falling into a loop of always picking the same, most OP kit. Instead it tries to add variety by selecting one load-out before starting a round, where you will get more (not round relevant) loot from. At least for me this was helpful to not always pick the same. Then, within a round, you also get forced to pick between quite different traits, forcing you, to change your play-style even within the same load-out.
2. It makes it very easy to play it after a long time (like one year) again. For nearly every interaction / trait / attack / special attack w/e is a tooltip on hover, which displays, what it exactly is, how to use it (e.g. long press O-button or short press X button ...). This way, even after a year, you can go straight back in.
3. The music makes it quite fun, by increasing the intensity through out the game from stage to stage. One round has multiple stages, where each stage results in a boss fight. At the beginning of a stage, the music is quite temperate and in contrast to that, you often get a cinema-like title at the end of a stage. Best example is probably stage 2 in the Underground region.

Twice as good as Hades, because it's literally twice the game. I have a couple hundred hours on the Switch version of this, and I've completed 32 fear and gotten 100% of the achievements for this game, so please don't let the hours played fool you.

Gameplay is incredibly smooth, though, if you're used to Hades 1, there are some jarring differences that will take some time to overcome. The dialogue is organic, immersive, and plentiful, just like in Hades 1. Scylla and the Sirens are my new favorite band, and the rest of the music is fantastic as well. 

The Magick system and Hexes replace Calls, but in an elegant and clever way. Holding Attack, Special, or Cast charges an Omega move, which uses Magick but also charges your Hex. Hexes have their own paths with unique abilities, and there is one Hex for each of the gods in the boon pool. 

A small downside to the game (and this is nearly trivial) is the sheer quantity of resources you need to collect to unlock the keepsakes, zones, and incantations to completely unlock everything. There are 40 or 50 different items you need to keep track of. Despite the implementation of a Forget-Me-Not incantation to help you, it isn't quite enough to prevent you from accidentally trading away something you end up needing for something, and there is no buyback option once they are traded away. 

On the other hand, "Oh no, you mean I need to do another run with my favorite weapon and familiar? What ever will I do?!" The joy of replaying the game far outweighs that meager downside.

I'll recommend this game because if you're considering it, you've likely played Hades first, and if you liked that, you'll probably enjoy the sequel too.

[b]Differences between Hades and Hades II[/b]
The game has the same core mechanics as the first one, with a few key differences. Some features are completely new, like having familiars (pets) for bonuses and gathering materials to craft upgrades or garden. Others are just aesthetic changes that serve the same purpose, like upgrading your stats through Arcana Cards instead of the Mirror of Night.

The biggest difference is that there are two distinct paths you can take each night: you can go up to the surface or down into the Underworld. You're needed in both places, as the conflict is unfolding on Olympus and in Tartarus at the same time. 

Each path has 4 regions leading to their own boss fights, and you have to clear both sides several times to finish the story. In the first game, you had to defeat Hades around 10 times to reach the end of the narrative, and here it's roughly the same amount combining both routes. However, there's a different learning curve for each path, and sometimes you're doing suicide runs to the surface (which is kinda harder) just to fetch some garlic or whatever before you can keep making progress down below, which can feel like a waste of time.

This sequel might be targeting the girlies, as it has a lot of cute pets, a gardening mechanic, a female MC with a lot of feelings, a witchy theme, singing sessions with Artemis, and all sorts of cute cozy elements that a lot of them will love.

[b]Gods, NPCs, and relationships[/b]
Having two separate paths is kinda annoying when you want to level up relationships with NPCs, as half of them are on your way up and the other half are on your way down. Same goes for boons: some gods and goddesses are exclusive to certain routes.

[b]Mel vs. Zag: The personality gap[/b]
I wanted to play this game because the original was ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ epic. Unfortunately, Mel's dull personality made it way less fun for me. It’s the main reason I’m not hyped about farming collectibles or grinding out the rest of the achievements after getting the credits (also, WHY are the credits unskippable? I had to sit through them for an eternity).

I know it's subjective, but Zagreus was hilarious. His sense of humor, sarcasm, and attitude toward the story are what made the first game so compelling for me. The SASS, the AUDACITY, and the vibes were immaculate. He'd talk smack to the KING of the underworld and crack jokes with Skelly all the time.

Mel takes everything way too seriously. Sure, this is her life's mission and it carries a different weight than Zag trying to escape, but it makes the journey feel way less fun and more like a burden. Again, total personal preference. I just didn't realize how much Zag carried the first game for me until I saw him in that dream through the mirror and immediately started grinning again.

The story was also less compelling to me. In the first game, I wanted Zag to reunite with his mother, and it was always emotional and felt like a huge triumph to get there. Here, grandpa Chronos is mad because he's a prick and his family hates him, so he decides to ruin everyone's lives. I wasn't a huge fan of how Mel handled him in the end either, but it fits her personality, so there's that.

[b]On the more positive side[/b]
The game's still really good, obviously. You have a lot of challenges and content to clear, plenty of new weapons to try, new gods and characters to meet, cool decor for the Crossroads, and a bit of extra story related to the first game.

So yeah, if you liked Hades and you ran out of things to do, or if you just want a change of scenery, this game is definitely worth trying out!

You don't need me to tell you that this is a worthy successor to the greatest rogue-lite of all time, returning with vast amounts of amazing gameplay and character interactions and voice acting. 

What I can say is that after having unlocked all achievements in just under 90 hours of playtime, the gameplay is still engaging, even if the voice lines do start to drag, especially when the game skips some early game lines if you progress too quickly, and only plays then way too late in the game for them to make sense. By no means a deal breaker, but for a game with such a focus on character interactions, you notice.

Supergiant have gone above and beyond to increment on their established formula in a genre stiff with competition. The core gameplay loop remains mostly unchanged with a few sorely needed additions but the same 10/10 rogue-lite’s roots are still relevant in Melinoe’s story as much as it was with Zaggreus’. Gamers looking for a narrative/story game will have a bittersweet experience, but Hades II is undoubtedly Supergiant and the rogue-lite genre at its best. 

One of the strongest things Hades II has going for it is the presentation and personality of its lovable cast of characters that are all incredibly memorable and even the interpretations make sense relative to narrative progression. Seeing figures like Hercules (Heracles), Odysseus, and Icarus brought to life is a really endearing experience and lovers of Greek mythology will find a lot to appreciate in the whole cast of minor and major characters, even with some minor growing pains. 

Though the characters themselves are a huge boon to the game and the impression it leaves, some of the bond forging steps/questlines are painfully convoluted. Narcissus/Echo, Arachne/Athena, and Heracles to list some examples. My understanding is the game is written in unobfuscated Lua and though I'd like to refrain from making this review too technical I was able to review a couple of code snippets to verify the guidance of these questlines on various sites (a reddit post, an achievement hunter forum, and Bing/Google search AI [of which produced surprisingly accurate summaries of the Arachne/Athena questline even after verifying with the logic]). 

My main concerns regarding the questlines are: Having to have a Narcissus encounter spawn then ignoring it, tying Athena/Arachne as well as Heracles quest progression to dialogue that is given a lower priority than story dialogue that has no impact outside of bonds, and in particular the Heracles questline requiring clearing multiple vow of rivals producing an arguably unreasonable skill curve for narrative focused players. 

For Narcissus it seems difficult to intuit the steps of the questline without essentially giving up and unintentionally progressing it. This might be feasible but you have to ignore a Narcissus encounter and then select an Echo encounter in the same run which feels like having your cake and eating it too, making it feel like dumb luck whether you can complete the questline without utilizing an online guide. Regarding the dialogue blocking quest progression: it makes sense during the main story/set of events to keep narrative cohesion and control the release of information to the player, however in the epilogue/post-story this provides a major barrier to progressing multiple questlines/bonds where adding logic that checks the flag for entering epilogue and prioritizes bond dialogue for players past the story would remove some rough spots in seeing all the content the game has to offer. Finally the vow of rivals, an optional difficulty modifier a player can toggle that makes the first X number of bosses much more difficult, is not only required to reach the end of the Heracles questline but a player has to complete at least 5 runs with the vow before they can make any progress in the questline at all. I believe that, without toggling God mode (damage reduction), such a feat would realistically be reserved for the top quartile of player and is unreasonable to narrative players to gatekeep interactions behind such a degree of difficulty, and rather detracts from the overall gameplay loop frankly. 

The core gameplay loop is undoubtedly phenomenal, but there are a few features that could've been added to make the game more complete for mid/end-game: Equipping custom boons in the training area of the crossroads to build test/theorycraft, some type of DPS measurer–perhaps an in-narrative character that appears after completing a minor prophecy–as well, a way to add surrounding targets to Schelemeus’ training ground to test AOEs, an optional elite enemy/boss gauntlet to skip specific areas/locations after beating a boss X number of times, and a little bit more reward for maxing out the bond of the merchants found throughout your run. 

To remediate merchants perhaps choosing their keepsakes until meeting them in the run gives some type of minor buff (Arachne might give you a passive that regenerates armor based on damage dealt, Narcissus might give an effect that drops X max number of boons at a Y% chance, Echo could give an effect that reduces damage taken at the cost of lowering the level of a random blessing Melinoe already has, etc.) which would give more strategic depth to keepsakes on top of the additional narrative harmony. While I do appreciate the familiarity and feeling of a learning curve with the same bosses, the late game recipes requiring beating a final boss require 20-30 mins of runback that feels more tedious than skill testing, and a sufficiently frustrated player is likely to turn on God mode anyway, removing any skill checks intended. Having the ability to quickly select boons and either fight the boss of a region or skip certain regions entirely would be a welcome change for skilled and inexperienced players alike and would additionally help keep the gameplay feeling fresh for that much longer without artificially extending gameplay. 

Though I do harbor reasonable critique of the narrative, the gameplay shines as brilliantly as Pallas Athena and the weapons are all varied and even different aspects (alternative versions of weapons with unique passive abilities) within weapon types can produce entirely unique runs. Even better then that the player doesn't need to change their playstyle for a weapon to be viable. Having a random weapon class give bonus resources that are useful both early and late game is a wonderful idea and naturally encourages the player to use different weapon types, and having certain optional boss dialogue tied to using a specific weapon or aspect provides a nice additional motivation for narrative-oriented players to continue using a variety of weapons.
 
I would temper this all by saying autofire probably could've been either enabled by default or a pop-up/in-game dialogue (presumably from Schelemeus) could explain it's a setting. Otherwise I have concerns about wear and tear of repeatedly pressing your mouse or a button on your controller for a 100+ hour game, but I understand there's an intrinsic balancing issue where the torch is meant to be the only weapon with autofire and for some weapons precision firing may be preferable. Perhaps a happy middle ground would be to offer a slower autofire option for non-torch weapons, or even charge mana per each autofire to add a strategic element without massively unbalancing the gameplay.

Probably one of the most attractive aspects of Hades II aside from the phenomenal gameplay is its sound: the music is impeccable. Supergiant truly shines when it comes to their soundtracks and the OST alone makes each run incredibly addictive, especially for faster players. Ranging from slow serenades in the crossroads to epic crunchy guitars in the final encounter leaves very little wonder as to why people keep coming back to Supergiant and their games. 

Overall then, Supergiant has produced an amazing game and rogue-lite. Some of its constraints felt limiting, but overall producing such incredible gameplay and cast of characters is more than attractive enough to draw in potential players and the transcendental music and fine-tuned combat create an amazing game that I could easily see any player put 100, 1000, or even 10,000 hours into Hades II easily.

I mean... I guess... I have to compare it to Hades which I've 100%'d because everyone else has...GEE WILLICKERS. I'm going to try not to do that. I really love Supergiant Games. I don't think they have ever released a terrible game in their existence. Most of their games are easily 9-10/10.

And this game is no different. It's definitely more difficult than the first game. I actually enjoyed this though. The art was cool, still great. But wasn't a fan of all the character's designs. The new characters were cool though. I feel the story was pretty good. The ending wasn't the greatest or anything but I don't think it deserves the criticisms it is receiving. There's really a bunch of ending if you think about it. Each side character has an ending of sort once you complete their storylines.

The combat issue isn't really a thing. You're kind of forced to get nectars and a lot of them so you can unlock the keepsakes. This requires a good amount of runs. If you don't do this making a build will feel almost impossible. Another difficulty aspect I don't mind. It's a roguelike I knew what I was getting into as I was purchasing the game. Once you have done enough runs and unlocked Weapon aspects, arcana, and the keepsakes, acquiring a build is very easy. You pick the weapon, and the keepsake of the God/Goddess you want to start with, and switch out the keepsake every level to ensure a greater success in that build coming to fruition. There's even an arcana that gives you 8 resets. So it's really not rocket science here. You just have to be patient. And sometimes you do not get EVERY boon for the build, but sometimes you end up with some pretty wild and random stuff that still pairs really well. It won't cripple you if you do not get EVERY single boon for the build.

There's a bunch of different areas that can be unlocked. So if it's ever getting boring for you, that will all change.  Just wake up Hypnos, do enough stuff for Chaos, and unlock the Oath of the Unseen. And it's a whole new experience and way more difficult than the base game. Again, totally fine with this.

The combat was cool. I have absolutely no issues with the combat. They tried something different than the first game and in my opinion it works out. You can't just button mash the hell out of the controller now and win like you could in the first game. You actually have to put some thought into how you will attack, where and when you will dash and Omega at. Plus you have to take into account which enemies you are actually fighting, their attacks, movement, and speed. Even sometimes you have to rely on the level for blocking. Pretty much you can't be a mindless ape while fighting. A-Ok with me.

There's some cool throwbacks to the first game. I won't mention them, but if you make it far enough and played Hades you will know them all. The personalities of the characters were done really well. I won't lie and say the story was immaculate or anything, but I didn't think it was terrible or anything. I still felt fulfilled beating the main story and able to continue playing after. It was a really cool mechanic to allow you to continue playing. At first I thought "how are they going to pull this off?" But it was really awesome.

The negative reviews are pretty much just stating that the game is different from their holy grail "Hades" and because it's literally not a carbon copy of the first game with a new skin they hate it. Now saying that I thought Hades deserved to win GOTY when it released. I did not feel that about Hades II, but it's a very solid 9.9/10. I've had an amazing time in my almost 80 hours. Don't let the naysayers nitpicking every minute semantic drive you away from trying a challenging game with different mechanics. It's totally worth the price. At 77 hours I've 50%'d the game. So I will definitely get my moneys worth if it takes around 160 hours to 100% the game. But let's be honest I already got it in 77 hours. And the fact that I still continue to want to play it is a plus.

Good job Supergiant Games! I look forward to your next release!

Hades II is like this gorgeous bottle of ambrosia, shining away right in front of you, and naturally you can’t wait to crack it open and have a taste. Then another taste. Then, well... let’s not pretend you were ever going to stop voluntarily.

Only, once you finally get into it, you discover it isn’t ambrosia after all. It’s nectar. Which is still perfectly respectable, obviously - nectar is good stuff! Except every other sip comes with this foul, frustrating aftertaste. As though nectar alone wasn’t quite enough, and someone topped up the bottle with whatever happened to be lying around, ruining what ought to be a truly magnificent drink.

Still, if nothing else, it’s seriously addictive. I’ll give it that! Though perhaps you’d be better off finding healthier indulgences - something a little less… disagreeable and fickle, maybe? Then again, I suppose most would call that aftertaste "character" and pour another. Even if you regret it later, it's still mostly nectar, so bottoms up, right? Just don’t say I didn’t warn you!

Topping the first game seemed like an almost impossible task, but Hades 2 really delivers where it counts. Fantastic and varied gameplay, tight story-telling and memorable music highlight this masterpiece of addicting fun. Highly recommended!
